content: Both of these metrics assign a value of 1 to each year of life lived in full health, while years lived with illness or disability are assigned values less than 1, depending on the severity of the condition. For instance, if a cancer treatment costs $1 million and provides, on average, two additional years of full health to a patient, the cost per QALY would be $500,000. This approach avoids the ethical and practical challenges of assigning a direct monetary value to human life, as is often required in other areas of economics. For example, stating that a treatment costs $5,000 per QALY does not imply any judgment about the monetary worth of a year of life or the subjective quality of that life. Another way to assess quality of life is by considering factors beyond health, such as the standard of living. For example, individuals living in rural areas or small towns often prefer to remain there, even if moving to a city would significantly increase their standard of living. This suggests that the quality of life associated with rural living is valued highly enough to outweigh the potential financial benefits of urban life. Similarly, jobs that negatively impact quality of life, such as night shifts or roles requiring extensive travel, typically offer higher salaries to compensate for these drawbacks. Much of this work focuses specifically on HRQoL rather than broader definitions of quality of life. The International Society for Quality of Life was established to support this area of research and serves as a valuable resource for information on the topic. Additionally, various organizations and research groups worldwide have made efforts to create standardized methods for assessing quality of life.
